hook.line: Throw five beans and move a pebble by the number that show their mark. The Aztecs played it for stakes.
hook.say: Woof! Let me show you the story of Patolli.

ch.t: A gambling game of the Aztecs
ch.say: It appears in records of the 16th century.
p: A gambling game of the Aztecs. Durán (16th century) describes an X-shaped board drawn with liquid rubber on a reed mat; he and Sahagún tell of red and blue pebbles for pieces and marked beans thrown as dice. The game is named after the beans (patolli).
People of every rank played it, for high stakes. Players called on Macuilxochitl (“Five Flower”), the god of games, as they threw. The Spanish banned the game and burned the mats and beans (Durán).

ch.t: Throw the beans, go once round
ch.say: A rounded square at the end of an arm: throw again!
ch.cap: The board of Bell’s reconstruction (60 squares). Drawn here as an upright cross; in play it lies as an X
p: Instead of dice you throw five beans and move as many squares as beans show their white mark. All five marked counts 10; none means no move.

Land on one of the eight rounded squares at the ends of the arms and you throw again. Land on one of the eight squares marked with a black triangle and you pay your rival 2. The game is played for stakes.

ch.say: You can play two rule sets here.
cards: Proposed by R. C. Bell (1960). 60 squares. Stakes go into a pool; you pay on marked squares and when stuck. No captures. The first to bring six home takes the pool.
The rules most often seen today. 52 squares. Only a 1 enters. Captures only on the four centre squares. Win by taking all of your rival’s stakes.

items: Durán writes that all five beans showing their mark counted as ten.
The pieces were twelve pebbles — six red and six blue, shared between the two players, as Durán and Sahagún record.
One theory holds that 52 squares stand for the 52-year calendar cycle. It is the archaeologist Caso’s interpretation; no source of the time says so.

cards: Where does the name come from?
The game is named after the beans that are thrown (patolli in Nahuatl).
What was the board drawn on?
According to Durán, the board was an X drawn with liquid rubber on a reed mat (petate).
Patolli was played for high stakes, by people of every rank.
Durán writes that the Spanish banned patolli and burned the mats and beans.
How pieces entered, which way they ran and how they went home is recorded nowhere. The rules here are the reconstruction R. C. Bell offered in 1960, with the warning that too little is known.
The accounts differ on the number of beans: in the sixteenth century Sahagún wrote of four, Durán of five or six. This game uses five.

p: Two players, six pieces each. Throw five beans, move by the number of marked ones, go once round the board, and be first to bring all six home. The original rules are lost: what you play here is a later reconstruction.
